title: The abuse crisis
hookLine: clergy abuse and cover-ups hurt children; survivors come first

cards: A note before we start. Today's lesson is about the abuse of children by clergy, and about leaders who covered it up. Nothing graphic is described.
If this touches your own life, you can stop here, or come back to it another day, and it's worth reaching out to someone you trust or a local support line.
For everyone else: this is part of the long story of the Church in our time, and leaving it out would be its own kind of cover-up.
Children and vulnerable adults were harmed by priests and religious they had every reason to trust.

teach.h: THE ABUSE, AND THEN THE COVER-UP.
teach.b: Four things, said carefully. First, the harm was double.

The abuse itself, then what came after: survivors who told the truth and were doubted, families pressured into silence, abusers sent somewhere new. Public reports and investigations described this pattern.
Second, who broke it open. Not, first of all, the Church's leaders.

Survivors, who kept telling their stories, often for years; journalists and investigators who listened; lay people and some clergy who refused to look away. Third, what the Church's leaders have said.
Pope Francis wrote to the whole Church admitting that the Church had not acted in time, and he quoted Paul, in the Douay-Rheims: "if one member suffer any thing, all the members suffer with it."
Catholics also hear a hard warning from Jesus: for anyone who leads one of these little ones astray, it would be better to be drowned in the sea with a millstone around the neck. Fourth, the word.

Safeguarding means the plain, unglamorous rules that protect children and vulnerable adults now: background checks, training, never one adult alone with a child, clear ways to report, and reporting to civil authorities.
Some dioceses and parishes now have a named safeguarding office. Survivors and their advocates say rules alone aren't enough without honesty and accountability, and that work isn't finished.
Through all of it, one principle: survivors first. Not the reputation of an institution. Not the comfort of the people in charge.

how: Catholic dioceses commonly have safeguarding offices and require background checks and training for clergy, staff and volunteers who work with children; some keep a day of prayer for survivors of abuse.

o: the rules and care that protect children now
a policy for keeping church files confidential
a fund that pays survivors after a court case

s: the crisis was only about individual abusers
the harm was double: abuse, and then leaders who covered it up.
Church leaders were the first to break the silence
survivors kept telling their stories, and journalists and investigators listened.
safeguarding includes clear ways to report to civil authorities
training, checks, never one adult alone with a child, and reporting.

games.q: you're on a parish council, and a family brings a concern about someone who works with children. what comes first?
o: believe and protect the child, and report it.
quietly move the person to another role.
games.why: today's line is survivors first: the child's safety, and reporting, before any reputation. moving abusers quietly is the pattern the cover-ups followed.

practice: You don't need to picture anything. Bring to mind the people, often unnamed, who were harmed as children and then not believed, and let them come first, not last.
If you pray, pray for their healing in whatever words you have; if not, hold them with respect.

wordCard.voice: Safeguarding. The work of protecting children and vulnerable adults: training, checks, clear reporting, and putting survivors first.

carryVoice: Your line: survivors first. This was a hard one, and you stayed with it. Go gently.
